title: The poor people's Bible
hook: colored windows told Bible stories to people who couldn't read

segments.voice: Yesterday, beads and knots: the rosary, and the Jesus Prayer said on a prayer rope. Your line was counting love.

Late afternoon, and a patch of blue and red light slides slowly across a stone floor. Follow it up to where it comes from, and there's a window high in the wall, made of small pieces of colored glass. Look closer, and the colors become people. A man in a boat. A woman at a well. A shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders. A whole story, told in light, pane by pane, from the bottom of the window to the top.

Stained glass gets its color as the glass is made. Then the details, faces, hands, the folds of a robe, are painted on with dark paint and fired so they hold, and lead strips join the pieces like the lines in a coloring book. In the great churches of the middle ages, windows like these told the Bible's stories, and the lives of the saints, to people who couldn't read. A pope, Gregory the Great, wrote to a bishop who had smashed the pictures in his church. Don't destroy them, Gregory told him: what writing gives to those who can read, a picture gives to those who can't. Some people later called windows like these the poor people's Bible. Some historians wonder how much anyone could make out of a window that high, but even from the floor, the light did its work. Windows often paired stories, one from the Old Testament beside one from the New, so that Jonah coming out of the fish sits near Jesus rising from the tomb. Often you read them from the bottom up. John writes, in the King James Bible, "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." A stained glass window is dark from the outside. You only see its story from inside, when the sun comes through. Christians haven't all loved these windows. In some times and places, reformers broke them, believing images drew worship away from God. Other Protestants kept them and made new ones, and churches of different traditions use them still.

segments.voice: If you can, find something colored and clear, a bottle, a glass of juice, a colored jar, even a phone screen set to a single color, and hold it up to a lamp or a window. Watch the color the light makes, and notice that the glass does nothing on its own; it waits for the light. If you pray, give thanks for the light; if you don't, simply watch it.
Stained glass. Colored glass, painted and leaded into windows that tell the Bible's stories in light, once called the poor people's Bible.
Your line: light tells stories. Pane by pane, the whole story comes into view. That's day eight hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Stained glass windows still tell Bible stories in churches of different traditions, and churches sometimes hold tours or talks that walk people through a window's story from bottom to top.

chat.says: Why do old churches have so many stained glass windows? Just decoration?
options: More than that. They told Bible stories and saints' lives to people who couldn't read.
Mostly to keep sunlight out, since worship was meant to happen in the dark.
Mostly to show off a town's wealth; the pictures weren't meant to teach anyone.
chat.meaning: Pope Gregory said a picture gives those who can't read what writing gives readers. Windows told the Bible's stories in light.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or quantities given; 'people who couldn't read' follows the outline hook.
Gregory's letter to Serenus paraphrased; reference number (Registrum 11.10, sometimes 11.13) needs a check.

'Biblia pauperum' properly names a later genre of block-book picture Bibles; the script says 'some people later called windows like these the poor people's Bible' and the original note says the name was 'later given to picture Bibles and windows like these'. Confirm fair.
Typological pairing (Jonah / Resurrection) is common in medieval windows; Matthew 12:40 supports the link. Confirm 'often'.
Glass technique (pot-metal color, painted and fired details, lead cames): confirm summary.
Iconoclasm: 'in some times and places, reformers broke them', with other Protestants keeping and making windows; ranks no one. Confirm.
Original is Latin, flagged as Latin in the note.
Editor: hook close fixed (it said 'today's word is the window'; the title is the poor people's Bible); garbled 'the way the light rises' replaced.
Editor 2: 'you read them from the bottom up' softened to 'often' (not true of every window); stock 'Settle, and breathe' cut.
Audit: 'fearing images' was an unfair, dismissive gloss on reformers' iconoclasm; now states their reason (concern that images drew worship from God). John 1:5 KJV checked.
